evals.prompt: Our monthly SDK digest for Petrel Labs (about 14,000 developers) started going to spam in June, right after we moved from our old newsletter tool to a new one. Opens went from 41% to 22%. Marketing wants to rewrite every subject line and drop the word 'free' from the free-tier section, since spam filters hate it. We also send password resets from petrel.dev, same as the newsletter. Here's what a June issue's header shows at Gmail: 'dkim=pass header.i=@mailer-cloud.net; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounces.mailer-cloud.net; dmarc=fail header.from=petrel.dev'. Can you just give us the new subject lines?
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses lost DMARC alignment after the platform move from the supplied header, refuses content-first fixes, discounts the open-rate drop, and gives a fix plan led by custom DKIM on the user's domain, with Postmaster Tools and a cohort ramp.
expectations: States that DMARC fails because DKIM and SPF pass only for the platform's domain (mailer-cloud.net), not petrel.dev
Names custom DKIM signing with d= on petrel.dev (or a subdomain of it) as the first technical fix
Declines to lead with subject-line rewrites or spam-word removal, and says content is checked only after authentication and reputation
Says the word 'free' or spam-word lists are not a meaningful filter factor at Gmail or Outlook
Says the open-rate drop alone is not evidence of spam-folder placement, citing mail-privacy features or image blocking
Asks for or recommends Gmail Postmaster Tools spam-rate data and marks complaints unverified until it exists
Says Gmail 4.7.x or 5.7.x authentication replies, if present in the bounce log, are sender-side and must not be suppressed
Recommends checking the raw bounce or deferral replies (for example 4.7.32 or other 4.7.x/5.7.x codes) rather than platform hard/soft totals
Mentions that the newsletter sharing petrel.dev with password resets puts reset mail at risk, and suggests moving the newsletter to a dedicated subdomain as a later step
Does not recommend buying a dedicated IP
Gives a fix plan where each row has an owner, a date and a done-when check
Includes a done-when check of a seed issue showing dkim=pass with the user's own domain and dmarc=pass
Orders the next send by most recent human clicks over consecutive sending days rather than one full send

evals.prompt: Quillwork (our open-source static site generator) has a community newsletter we haven't sent since February. 11,400 subscribers, all from the signup form on our docs site. v3.0 ships next Tuesday and we want everyone to hear about it. To be safe we already paid a list-cleaning service, which removed 1,600 'risky' addresses, so we're down to 9,800 'verified'. Plan is to send the announcement to all 9,800 Tuesday morning at 9am. Any last checks before we hit send?
evals.expected_output: Stops the single blast to a list dormant for eight months, explains recycled traps and that verification cannot find them, and plans a cohort ramp starting with the most recently engaged, with hold rules, a re-permission step for the cold tail, and a realistic Tuesday plan.
expectations: Applies a re-confirmation issue for a list silent this long (or names the programme's silent-list rule as the deciding fact), sent through the ramp with non-responders suppressed
Explains that addresses dead during the silent months can have become recycled spam traps
States that a list-verification or cleaning service cannot reliably detect spam traps or prove readers still want the mail
Proposes sending Tuesday's issue first to the most recently engaged cohort (for example recent clickers or newest signups)
Describes growing cohorts over several sends (roughly doubling, or over weeks) rather than one send
Names concrete hold conditions between cohorts, such as user-unknown bounces around 2%, deferral spikes, or Gmail spam rate above 0.1%
Labels the 2% bounce hold level as a house rule, not a provider rule
Treats the 1,600 addresses the cleaning service removed as unproven cold-cohort subscribers, not as bounces
Sends the launch issue on Tuesday to the warm cohorts only and the rest over the following sending days
Asks whether click history exists to order cohorts, or says to fall back to signup date when it does not
Recommends reading each send's raw bounce replies before the next cohort
Does not recommend buying a dedicated IP or switching platform for the launch
Checks authentication (DKIM and DMARC alignment) of the sending domain before the restart

evals.prompt: The Fernhill CLI weekly digest has ~22,000 subscribers, around 60% at big companies. We run self-hosted listmonk sending through Amazon SES from digest@fernhill.dev, which also sends our password resets. Since August, readers at enterprise companies keep emailing us that they got unsubscribed without clicking anything, and our click-through went from 4% to 11% even though nothing about the content changed. Ops says the unsubscribe link is GET /unsubscribe?u=<base64 of the email>. Our Gmail open rate also fell to 18%, so I assume we're in spam at Gmail too. What's going on?
evals.expected_output: Identifies corporate link scanners fetching a GET unsubscribe URL as the cause of false unsubscribes and inflated clicks, fixes the endpoint to POST-only with an opaque token and RFC 8058 headers, discounts the open-rate claim, and handles the wrongly removed readers without silent re-adding.
expectations: Explains that corporate security gateways or link scanners fetch URLs on arrival and thereby trigger the GET unsubscribe
Explains the click-rate jump as scanner or bot clicks rather than real engagement
Recommends making the unsubscribe act only on POST, with GET showing a confirmation page
Gives a test order: GET the URL, confirm the seed is still subscribed, then POST, then confirm it is unsubscribed
Warns that the confirmation page must not auto-submit with JavaScript because some scanners execute it
Flags that a base64-encoded email in the URL lets anyone unsubscribe anyone, and recommends an opaque token checked server-side
Recommends List-Unsubscribe with an HTTPS URI plus List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click
States that the List-Unsubscribe headers must be covered by the DKIM signature (h= tag)
Says the unsubscribe endpoint must not return a redirect to the POST
Says the 18% open rate is not evidence of Gmail spam placement
Recommends filtering scanner clicks (seconds after delivery, cloud IPs, every link clicked) before reporting clicks or applying an inactivity rule
Says not to silently re-subscribe the readers removed by scanners, and to tell them how to resubscribe or restore only those who ask
Puts fixing the unsubscribe endpoint first in the fix plan
Suggests verifying the scanner hypothesis by comparing unsubscribe or click timestamps with delivery time
Mentions that sharing fernhill.dev with password resets is a later separation step (dedicated newsletter subdomain)

evals.prompt: Our security team at Corvane wants to publish 'v=DMARC1; p=reject; pct=10' on corvane.com next Monday and ramp pct up weekly. We don't have DMARC at all today and no reports. Mail going out as corvane.com: Google Workspace for staff, our developer newsletter through a newsletter platform, Zendesk for support, invoices from our billing system, and Greenhouse for recruiting. The newsletter person (me) is worried. Is their plan fine?
evals.expected_output: Rejects the pct-based reject-first plan, explains pct removal in RFC 9989 and the t=y replacement, and lays out monitor, inventory, subdomain-first enforcement, organizational domain last.
expectations: States that the pct tag was removed by RFC 9989 (DMARCbis) because receivers applied partial values inconsistently
Names t=y test mode as the replacement for pct
Recommends rehearsing each enforcement level with t=y together with pct=0 so old and new receivers both apply one level lower
Recommends reading aggregate reports for a period (weeks) before any enforcement
Lists inventorying every sender (Workspace, newsletter platform, Zendesk, billing, Greenhouse) and aligning or retiring each
Warns that p=reject without inventory would make legitimate third-party mail (such as invoices or support replies) fail
Recommends enforcing on the newsletter subdomain before the organizational domain
Recommends the newsletter platform sign with custom DKIM on the corvane domain or its subdomain
Notes that some receivers may still follow the old RFC 7489 behaviour during the transition
Describes t=y as an on/off test flag rather than a percentage ramp
Gives the order: monitor, inventory, subdomain enforcement, organizational domain enforcement

evals.prompt: I run a solo weekly dev newsletter (Pebbleworth Weekly), 4,200 subscribers. I send it from my personal address, jonah.pebble@gmail.com, through a newsletter platform because I like replies landing in my inbox. My product app at pebbleworth.app also sends about 3,000 notification emails a day. Since I'm under 5,000 a day, I figure Gmail's bulk sender rules don't apply to me. The platform is pushing a dedicated IP add-on so 'other senders can't hurt me'. Worth it?
evals.expected_output: Corrects the freemail From, explains Gmail's primary-domain counting and permanence, and advises against a dedicated IP for a small weekly list, recommending an owned-domain subdomain with custom DKIM on the shared pool.
expectations: Says sending From a gmail.com address through a third-party platform cannot align DKIM or SPF to gmail.com
Mentions that Google warns it will apply DMARC quarantine to Gmail From impersonation, or that freemail domains like yahoo.com publish p=reject
Recommends sending the newsletter from a domain the user owns (pebbleworth.app or a subdomain of it)
Notes Reply-To can still point to the personal inbox so replies keep arriving there
Explains that Gmail counts mail to personal Gmail accounts from the same primary domain, including subdomains, toward the 5,000 a day, and only that Gmail-consumer share
Explains that once a domain reaches bulk status at Gmail it stays bulk permanently
Says to estimate the Gmail-consumer share of the newsletter plus the 3,000 daily notifications before deciding whether the domain is a bulk sender
Advises against the dedicated IP for a 4,200-subscriber weekly list
Explains that one weekly burst then silence is inconsistent volume that hurts a dedicated IP's reputation
Recommends staying on the platform's shared pool with custom DKIM on the user's own domain
Recommends a dedicated newsletter subdomain separate from the app's notification mail
Recommends a warm-up for the new sending domain or subdomain

evals.prompt: After last Thursday's send of the Saltmarsh Devs digest our newsletter platform flagged 1,930 'hard bounces' and wants us to delete them. Almost all are outlook.com and hotmail.com with '550 5.7.515 Access denied, sending domain saltmarshdevs.io does not meet the required authentication level'. Another 140 say '550 5.1.1 user unknown'. Also Gmail Postmaster Tools shows our spam rate at 0.4% - can you tell us how to find and remove the Gmail people who reported us?
evals.expected_output: Splits the bounces by code: suppress the 140 5.1.1, keep the 1,930 5.7.515 and fix authentication for Outlook.com; explains Gmail has no per-message complaint report, the 0.3% mitigation consequence, and prevention steps.
expectations: Gives a way to find which segment drives the Gmail spam rate: Feedback-ID feedback-loop data where the platform supports it, or sending cohorts on separate days and comparing Postmaster's daily rate
Recommends NOT deleting or suppressing the 1,930 5.7.515 addresses
Explains 5.7.515 as Outlook.com rejecting the sender for failing its authentication requirement, not bad addresses
Names the fix for 5.7.515 as SPF, DKIM and DMARC passing and aligned on the sending domain
Says the 5.7.515 readers can be reached again after the fix
States that Gmail provides no per-message complaint feedback, so individual complainers cannot be identified
States that at a Gmail spam rate above 0.3% the sender is ineligible for Google mitigation until 7 consecutive days below it
Gives 0.1% as the target spam rate
Recommends prevention levers instead: pausing the segment driving complaints, a working one-click unsubscribe, the inactivity rule
Asks what changed recently (import, old segment, new form) to explain the complaint spike
Recommends reading bounce reply text rather than the platform's hard/soft label
Recommends stopping or slowing sends to the complaining segment before other fixes
Says to pause and escalate a receiver only if it still blocks two sends after the authentication fix is verified

evals.prompt: Our Tidewater API changelog newsletter is in Gmail's Promotions tab and I hate it. Also MXToolbox says ourdomain is on 4 blocklists (UCEPROTECT and some others), though Spamhaus shows nothing. A company emailed offering to get us delisted from all of them for $299. And our inbox-placement seed test came back 92%, so honestly I think we're fine apart from Promotions. What tricks get us into Primary?
evals.expected_output: Explains Promotions is an inbox category not spam, declines tricks, says minor blocklists in mass checkers rarely matter and Spamhaus removal is free and follows fixing the cause, refuses paid delisting, and explains seed tests are directional only.
expectations: Recommends Spamhaus's own lookup page rather than DNS queries through public resolvers, or warns that public-resolver lookups return misleading codes
Declines to give tricks for escaping Promotions, noting they risk complaints
Suggests the only sanctioned lever is asking readers to move the message or reply
Says most lists flagged by mass blocklist checkers are irrelevant to Gmail and Outlook placement
Identifies Spamhaus (and its domain list) as the listing that matters, and notes it is clean here
Explains Gmail Postmaster Tools spam rate below 0.1% as the target figure to check
States that delisting requests are made by the sender, free of charge, after fixing the cause
Explains seed or placement tests are directional because seed inboxes have no engagement history
Recommends Gmail Postmaster Tools spam rate as the real placement evidence
Says requesting delisting before fixing the cause leads to being listed again
Does not claim the newsletter is in the spam folder based on the Promotions placement
Checks or asks about authentication and one-click unsubscribe status before concluding all is fine

evals.prompt: Readers of the Larchmont Data newsletter who work at big enterprises (we hear from banks and a couple of Fortune 500s) say our issues land in Junk or quarantine, while personal Gmail readers get it fine. Postmaster Tools shows 0.04% spam rate and DMARC passes. My CEO wants us to switch to a different newsletter platform next month to fix it. Good idea?
evals.expected_output: Points to corporate gateways (Microsoft Defender BCL, Safe Links, other gateways) as a separate filter Gmail data cannot show, advises against a platform switch, asks for reader headers, and gives allow-listing and feed fallbacks.
expectations: Explains that corporate mail gateways filter separately from consumer Gmail, so a good Postmaster Tools reading says nothing about them
Names Microsoft Defender's Bulk Complaint Level and its default threshold of 7 moving bulk mail to Junk
Mentions that the Strict preset uses threshold 5 and quarantines, which fits regulated enterprises such as banks
Notes that the Standard preset uses threshold 6
Mentions that company admins can lower the bulk threshold
Recommends asking an affected reader for the message headers (for example X-Forefront-Antispam-Report with BCL) before acting
Advises against switching platforms as the fix, noting a switch resets signals and needs a warm-up
Recommends publishing allow-listing instructions for readers' IT teams naming the sending domain and DKIM d= rather than IPs
Recommends a consistent branded HTTPS tracking domain or no tracking
Offers a feed or web archive fallback for readers whose company junks bulk mail
Mentions that Google Workspace corporate recipients fall outside Gmail's sender rules and follow their admins' policies
Notes that gateway link scanning can inflate clicks and recommends filtering them
Does not treat the corporate Junk placement as a list-quality or consent problem without evidence
Gives a monitoring or evidence step with an owner rather than a vague recommendation
